subject: music
title: Hyperpop: PC Music, Sophie, 100 gecs and Brat (2013–2024)
dek: In 2013 a London music student named A. G. Cook started uploading songs to SoundCloud under the name PC Music. They sounded like adverts, ringtones and chart pop from 2004 played too fast and too bright. Ten years later that sound, now called hyperpop, had passed through a viral duo from St. Louis, a Spotify playlist, TikTok during the pandemic and a lime-green album cover that ended up on a presidential campaign.
era: About 2013 to 2024, with roots in Eurodance, trance, J-pop and Auto-Tune pop, and effects on the online microgenres that followed
honesty: This lesson keeps to dates, names and events documented in the English Wikipedia articles on hyperpop, PC Music, A. G. Cook, Sophie (musician), Oil of Every Pearl's Un-Insides, 100 Gecs, Money Machine, Charli XCX, Brat (album), Digicore, Glaive, Dorian Electra, Arca, Hannah Diamond, Kero Kero Bonito, Bladee, Kyary Pamyu Pamyu, Yasutaka Nakata, Hatsune Miku, Auto-Tune and Believe (Cher song). Short quotations come from those articles, which cite the original reviews and interviews. The analysis sections are my own summary, not claims from a single source.

timeline.label: Auto-Tune and the Cher effect
timeline.detail: Antares releases Auto-Tune in September 1997 as a tool to correct off-key singing. Cher's Believe (1998) uses it on purpose to make her voice sound robotic, and the sound becomes known as the 'Cher effect'.

timeline.label: Hatsune Miku
timeline.detail: Crypton Future Media releases Hatsune Miku in Japan, a Vocaloid singing-voice program sold with a cartoon character. A fully synthetic pop star becomes normal for a generation of fans.

timeline.label: PC Music and Bipp
timeline.detail: A. G. Cook founds PC Music in London in June and starts posting songs on SoundCloud. Sophie releases the single Bipp the same year, and it tops XLR8R's year-end list.

timeline.label: Hey QT and Lemonade
timeline.detail: Cook, Sophie and Hayden Dunham release Hey QT as the project QT, built around a fictional energy drink. Sophie's Lemonade/Hard follows. PC Music's first paid download, Hannah Diamond's Every Night, arrives in November. Spin calls PC Music its trend of the year.

timeline.label: Volume 1 and Product
timeline.detail: PC Music releases its first compilation, PC Music Volume 1, and signs a partnership with Columbia Records. Sophie gathers her singles on Product.

timeline.label: Charli XCX joins in
timeline.detail: Charli XCX releases the Vroom Vroom EP, mainly produced by Sophie, then the mixtapes Number 1 Angel and Pop 2 with Cook as executive producer. In October 2017 Sophie releases It's Okay to Cry, the first time her own voice and face appear in her work, and confirms she is transgender.

timeline.label: Oil of Every Pearl's Un-Insides
timeline.detail: Sophie's album comes out in June and is nominated for the Grammy for Best Dance/Electronic Album. Spotify analyst Glenn McDonald adds 'hyperpop' to the platform's genre metadata.

timeline.label: Money Machine and the playlist
timeline.detail: 100 gecs release Money Machine and the album 1000 gecs in May. In August Spotify editor Lizzy Szabo launches the Hyperpop playlist.

timeline.label: Lockdown boom
timeline.detail: During COVID-19 lockdowns, hyperpop and digicore spread through SoundCloud, Discord, Minecraft festivals and Alt TikTok. Charli XCX makes how i'm feeling now at home, and Cook releases 7G and Apple.

timeline.label: Loss and 'rip hyperpop?'
timeline.detail: Sophie dies in Athens on 30 January after a fall. In August Charli XCX tweets 'rip hyperpop? discuss', and several young artists say the label is dead.

timeline.label: PC Music closes
timeline.detail: On its tenth anniversary in June, PC Music announces that 2023 will be its last year of new releases.

timeline.label: Brat summer
timeline.detail: Charli XCX's Brat comes out on 7 June. Its lime-green cover becomes a meme, Kamala Harris's campaign copies the style, and Collins English Dictionary names 'brat' its word of the year. Sophie's second album, finished by her brother Benny Long, is released.

fun_fact.title: An energy drink that did not exist
fun_fact.text: In 2014 A. G. Cook, Sophie and the performance artist Hayden Dunham released Hey QT under the name QT. The project came with a fictional energy drink, the QT Energy Elixir, and at Sophie's request the song repeats the drink's name as product placement for a product nobody could buy. The joke came full circle the same year: Sophie's song Lemonade was later used in a real McDonald's commercial in 2015. Sophie once told Billboard that the genre of music she made was 'advertising'.

sections.title: Before hyperpop: robot voices, Eurodance and the internet

blocks.text: Hyperpop did not invent the idea of a machine-made pop voice. In 1997 the American company Antares released Auto-Tune, software meant to quietly fix singers who were slightly off key. A year later Cher's Believe turned the correction all the way up so that her voice jumped between notes like a robot, and the sound became known as the Cher effect. Through the 2000s artists such as Daft Punk, T-Pain and Kanye West made Auto-Tune a normal part of pop and hip-hop.

In Japan, the company Crypton Future Media released Hatsune Miku in August 2007. Miku is a Vocaloid voicebank, a program that sings any melody you type into it, sold with a cartoon character of a sixteen-year-old girl with turquoise twintails. She later performed concerts as a projected animation. In 2011 Kyary Pamyu Pamyu, a model from the Harajuku fashion scene, released Pon Pon Pon, written and produced by Yasutaka Nakata, who also produced the group Perfume. Kyary's music was sugary, fast and openly artificial, and her videos went viral in the West.

Writers also point to Western precursors. The Hyperpop article lists the nu rave band Test Icicles, the producers Rustie and Hudson Mohawke, Sleigh Bells, 3OH!3, the London musician Max Tundra, Kesha's half-spoken vocals, Britney Spears's 2011 dance singles and M.I.A.'s album /\/\ /\ Y /\ (2010). Fans of nightcore, a style of YouTube remix that speeds up songs and raises their pitch, were already using the word 'hyperpop' in the late 2000s. The earliest known use of the word is older still: in October 1988 the writer Don Shewey used it in an article about the Scottish band Cocteau Twins.

sections.title: PC Music: a record label as an art project

blocks.text: A. G. Cook, born Alexander Guy Cook in 1990, studied music at Goldsmiths, University of London, where he made music with his friend Danny L Harle. In June 2013 he founded PC Music, which at first existed mainly as a SoundCloud page. Within about a year it had posted 40 songs, some with more than 100,000 plays, without releasing a single physical record. Its first paid download was Hannah Diamond's Every Night in November 2014.

The label's sound took the shiniest parts of 1990s and 2000s pop and pushed them further. The Guardian heard 'the huge synth blasts favoured by Eurodance chart-botherers such as Cascada, grime's sub-bass, and happy hardcore's high-pitched vocal range'. Cook has named Korean and Japanese pop, Japanese gyaru culture, and the producers Max Martin and Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis as influences. Vocals were pitched up and chopped until they sounded like cartoons. The label often recorded people who were not trained singers and, in Cook's words, treated them 'as if they're a major label artist'.

PC Music behaved less like a band and more like a long-running piece of conceptual art. Many acts were aliases, so it was hard to tell how many people were involved. Artists such as Hannah Diamond, GFOTY (short for Girlfriend of the Year), Danny L Harle and Easyfun had invented personas built from internet slang and cartoon imagery. Songs borrowed the language of advertising, makeup hauls and corporate branding, so critics could never be sure whether the label was celebrating consumer culture or mocking it. Vice described the acts as 'living installations who put out music'. Critics later called this early PC Music sound bubblegum bass, and Pitchfork counts it as hyperpop's first era.

Reaction in 2014 was sharply divided. Spin named PC Music its trend of the year and Fact called it the best label of 2014, while other critics found the high-speed trance sound artless or irritating. In October 2015 the label announced a partnership with Columbia Records, and in December it released Only You, a collaboration between Cook and the Chinese pop star Chris Lee (李宇春).

sections.title: Sophie: sounds like latex, metal and bubbles

blocks.text: Sophie Xeon was born in 1985 in Northampton, England. Her father took her to raves when she was very young and played rave cassettes in the car, and her favourite acts were the Pet Shop Boys and the Prodigy. Her single Bipp (2013) was the breakthrough: it topped XLR8R's year-end list and placed 17th on Pitchfork's. Lemonade and Hard followed in 2014, and the singles were collected on Product in 2015.

Sophie built her sounds almost entirely from scratch. Working mainly with an Elektron Monomachine synthesiser and the software Ableton Live, she avoided samples and shaped basic waveforms into sounds she described as resembling 'latex, balloons, bubbles, metal, plastic, [and] elastic'. The Guardian wrote that her work sounded as if 'Aphex Twin had swallowed a 12-year-old girl's Spotify account', yet still 'spoke of heartache and yearning'. The New York Times called it 'giddy fun' that also invited listeners 'to consider pop's pleasures, structures and gender expectations'.

For years Sophie hid her identity. She masked her voice in interviews, obscured herself in photos, and at one Boiler Room show the drag performer Ben Woozy mimed a DJ set as Sophie while she posed as a bodyguard. In October 2017 she released It's Okay to Cry, the first time her own voice and image appeared in her work, and she confirmed that she was transgender. Her album Oil of Every Pearl's Un-Insides followed in June 2018. The title may be a mishearing of 'I love every person's insides'. It was nominated for the Grammy for Best Dance/Electronic Album, which made Sophie one of the first openly transgender artists nominated in that category.

Sophie also produced for Charli XCX, Vince Staples, Kim Petras, Madonna, the Japanese singer Namie Amuro and the K-pop group Itzy, and worked with Kyary Pamyu Pamyu in 2014. On 30 January 2021, aged 34, she died after falling from a rooftop in Athens, Greece, where she had climbed to take a photograph of the full moon. Her second album, almost finished when she died, was completed by her brother Benny Long and released in 2024. On her birthday that year, 17 September, Google ran a Doodle in her honour.

sections.title: Charli XCX brings the underground to pop

blocks.text: Charli XCX, born Charlotte Aitchison in 1992, started posting songs on Myspace in 2008 at the age of 14 and was soon booked for illegal warehouse raves in East London. Her stage name came from her old MSN Messenger display name. She first reached a mass audience as a writer and guest singer: Icona Pop's I Love It (2012) and Iggy Azalea's Fancy (2014) were both huge hits, and her own Boom Clap reached the US top ten in 2014.

In 2015 she began working with Sophie and the PC Music circle, which critics mark as the turning point of her career. The Vroom Vroom EP (2016), produced mainly by Sophie, had a harder, stranger Eurodance sound than anything she had made before. Number 1 Angel and Pop 2 (both 2017), with A. G. Cook as executive producer, mixed her chart instincts with producers such as Sophie, Umru and Easyfun. Vice later called her the 'queen' of the style, and Pop 2 in particular set a template for what hyperpop would sound like.

Charli became the link between an underground art scene and the mainstream. She could get PC Music producers onto major-label records and festival stages, while the producers gave her a sound that no other pop star had.

100 gecs are Dylan Brady and Laura Les, who grew up a few miles apart near St. Louis, Missouri. They first recorded together in Les's Chicago apartment in the winter of 2015 and self-released an EP in 2016. After a well-received DJ set at the 2019 Minecraft festival Fire Festival, they released their debut album 1000 gecs on 31 May 2019, with Money Machine as its single. The Independent said they took hyperpop 'to its most extreme, and extremely catchy, conclusions: stadium-sized trap beats processed and distorted to near-destruction, overwrought emo vocals and cascades of ravey arpeggios'. Jon Caramanica of The New York Times called it the best album of 2019.

The genre name itself came out of data. Glenn McDonald, a Spotify analyst who ran the genre map Every Noise at Once, said he first saw 'hyperpop' used about PC Music in 2014 and added it to Spotify's metadata in 2018. In August 2019 the Spotify editor Lizzy Szabo noticed the tag and launched a playlist called Hyperpop, which featured 100 gecs, A. G. Cook, Slayyyter, Caroline Polachek, Hannah Diamond and Kim Petras. Szabo called Cook the 'godfather' of the style. When Cook guest-curated the playlist that November and added artists such as J Dilla, Nicki Minaj and Kate Bush, smaller artists complained that they were being pushed off a playlist they relied on for income.

This is an unusual origin for a music genre. Earlier scenes in these lessons, such as Chicago house or riot grrrl, were named by the people in a club, a zine or a newspaper. Hyperpop's name was attached partly by a streaming service's database, and many artists only learned they belonged to it when they were added to the playlist.

The COVID-19 lockdowns of 2020 gave hyperpop its biggest moment. Teenagers stuck at home made music on laptops and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where a former strategy manager noticed a spike of new creators in March and April 2020. Concerts moved into Minecraft: 100 gecs headlined the Square Garden festival in April 2020 with Charli XCX, Kero Kero Bonito, Dorian Electra and Cashmere Cat. Cook ran free festivals over Zoom and Twitch and gave VIP ticket money to the transgender youth charity Mermaids and the Black Cultural Archives. In Los Angeles a party called Subculture held six-hour 'hyperpop raves' on Zoom with more than 1,000 guests at its peak.

Next to hyperpop grew digicore, a scene of mostly teenage rappers and producers who met on Discord. In 2018 a figure called Dalton started a Minecraft and Discord server called Loser's Club, which became a hub for artists including Glaive, Ericdoa, Quinn and Midwxst. Glaive, born in 2005, posted songs to SoundCloud at the start of the pandemic, signed with Interscope Records and released his debut EP Cypress Grove in 2020 at about fifteen. On TikTok, the community known as Alt TikTok spread the sound further. ElyOtto's SugarCrash! (2021) was used in more than five million TikTok videos.

items: Founders and first wave: A. G. Cook, Sophie, Hannah Diamond, GFOTY, Danny L Harle, Easyfun, QT, Charli XCX.
Second wave: 100 gecs, Dorian Electra, Slayyyter, Kim Petras, Caroline Polachek, Kero Kero Bonito, Umru, Ayesha Erotica.
Digicore and glitchcore: Glaive, Ericdoa, Quinn, Midwxst, Jane Remover, Yungster Jack and David Shawty, the collectives Helix Tears and Novagang.
Close neighbours: Arca, Bladee and his collective Drain Gang.

blocks.text: Hyperpop was strongly tied to queer culture. Sophie was a trans woman. Dorian Electra, whose albums Flamboyant (2019) and My Agenda (2020) play with masculinity as a costume, is genderfluid and uses they/them pronouns. Arca, a Venezuelan producer who has worked with Björk, Kanye West and FKA Twigs, has explored non-binary identity in her music since coming out in 2018. Because so much of the genre treats the voice as something to pitch up, pitch down and reshape, many artists used it to play with how gender sounds, and some listeners have said it helped them think about their own dysphoria.

Most earlier music movements in these lessons fought against something fake. Punk rejected polished stadium rock, and folk revivalists looked for authentic songs. Hyperpop did the opposite. Its maximalism took the most artificial parts of pop, such as Auto-Tune, ringtone melodies, advertising slogans and plastic textures, and made them louder until they became the point. The Wall Street Journal's Mark Richardson described it as turning pop's artificial parts up to an extreme, a 'cartoonish wall of noise'.

Under the brightness, the lyrics were often sad, anxious or ironic, which is why many listeners heard hyperpop as music about life lived online. NPR's Sheldon Pearce described it as music 'seeking the sound of the dissociated online self'. When so much of daily life happens through screens, filters and avatars, a voice that is obviously processed may feel more honest than one that pretends to be natural.

items: What hyperpop changed: it made artificiality and excess into a serious artistic position rather than a guilty pleasure.
It gave trans and non-binary artists a central place in a pop movement, and it used vocal processing to question how a 'male' or 'female' voice should sound.
It showed that a scene could form almost entirely online, through SoundCloud, Discord, Minecraft and TikTok, without a local club or city at its centre.
Its limits: the name was partly applied by Spotify, the label quickly became a catch-all for any loud internet pop, and many of its most inventive young artists rejected it or did not want fame.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: Hyperpop's conversation with East Asia went in both directions. PC Music borrowed openly from J-pop, K-pop and kawaii culture, and Kero Kero Bonito, a London band formed in 2011, recruited its singer Sarah Midori Perry through a bulletin board for Japanese expatriates. Perry, who is of mixed Japanese and British heritage, sings and raps in both languages, and the band's early work was influenced by Kyary Pamyu Pamyu.

Asian pop stars in turn hired hyperpop producers. Cook worked with Chris Lee in China in 2015 and co-produced Hikaru Utada's One Last Kiss in 2021, the theme for the anime film Evangelion: 3.0+1.0 Thrice Upon a Time. Sophie produced for Namie Amuro and for Itzy. In the early 2020s hyperpop scenes began to grow in Asia, and Billboard and Dazed named the Japanese artist 4s4ki as an important figure. Later, the related style dariacore found a cult following in Japan through the netlabel Lost Frog Productions, helped by Japan's existing culture of remixes and OtoMAD meme videos.

In Sweden, Bladee and Drain Gang, formed in 2013, were making a cloudy, Auto-Tuned rap that ran parallel to PC Music and later fed into digicore and glitchcore. In Spain, Nylon named Putochinomaricón one of the biggest names in the scene. Putochinomaricón is Chenta Tsai Tseng (蔡承達), a Taiwanese-born Spanish musician and architect who started in Madrid's alternative scene in 2018 and took the stage name from the racist and homophobic insults shouted at them in the street. In America and Britain, the same years saw streaming replace downloads and TikTok become the main place where songs broke, which is the world hyperpop both reflected and depended on.

By 2021 the label had stretched so wide that it was losing meaning. In August Charli XCX tweeted 'rip hyperpop? discuss'. Underscores said the genre was 'officially dead', and Glaive said he and Ericdoa were 'working on killing' it, before saying three months later that it 'will never die'. In June 2023, on its tenth anniversary, PC Music announced that it would stop releasing new music. Its final release was Thy Slaughter's album Soft Rock in December 2023.

Then hyperpop's ideas reached the biggest audience they ever had. Charli XCX's Brat, released on 7 June 2024 and produced with A. G. Cook, Finn Keane and others, drew on 2000s English rave music. Its cover was a plain square of what Charli called 'an offensive, off-trend shade of green' with the word brat in lowercase Arial. A fan-made generator let anyone put their own words on it, and 'Brat summer' became a meme. After Charli tweeted 'kamala IS brat', Kamala Harris's campaign account restyled its banner in the same green, though Charli later said the tweet was not meant as a political endorsement. Brat became Metacritic's highest-rated album of 2024, Collins English Dictionary made 'brat' its word of the year, and the album won three Grammy Awards, including Best Dance/Electronic Album, the category Sophie had been nominated in six years earlier.

Hyperpop's influence continues in newer online microgenres such as rage, jerk and sigilkore, and in the vocal processing that is now ordinary across pop. In 2025 Google ran a Doodle celebrating the genre for Pride Month.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: PC Music made consumer culture its subject: fake energy drinks, brand names and advert jingles, so that listeners could never be sure if it was praising shopping or mocking it. cool dairy also sells things, but for a cause. How would you talk about buying and selling in your shop's voice so that it feels playful and honest rather than either preachy or purely commercial?
